rule: the presence of a CPU read is NOT evidence that a field is a game resource and is never promoted to GAME_COST_EVIDENCED. A field read by HUD code, animation or a timer produces reads too.
startStateNote: every run starts from ONE canonical post-boot saved state per fixture, because this instrument randomises power-on RAM (B0 row 9). Runs are therefore comparable within this core; they are NOT comparable with an independent jsnes cold start, which B2 must handle explicitly.
pcProvenance: a sampled PC is the NEXT instruction address. The accessing instruction is resolved through disassembly, never by subtracting a constant (B1 prerequisites).

latchVersusResource.question: does the trace separate a genuine one-unit resource from a latch?
latchVersusResource.addressesDifferButThatIsNotADiscriminati: different variables are read by different instructions in any program. A difference in site ADDRESS says nothing about whether a field is a resource; only a difference in the STRUCTURE of its access could.

underTheThreeOwnDriverRegimes.why: all three regimes press only the field own driving button, so a consumer gated on a different button never runs

underTheConsumerRegime.why: singleUnit is read by the play-gated routine and oneShotSwitch is not, so a schedule that drives that routine separates them

latchVersusResource.verdict: SEPARATED, BUT ONLY BY A SCHEDULE THAT EXERCISES THE CONSUMER. Under the three regimes that press the field own driver the two are identical in writes, read counts and reader-site count. Adding the play button - which drives a routine that reads singleUnit and never reads oneShotSwitch - separates them. The first negative was a property of my action schedule, not of the instrument.
latchVersusResource.whatThisStillDoesNotEstablish: that singleUnit is a game resource. An extra read from a distinct instruction is a LEAD about a consumer; it is not evidence of a game cost and is never promoted to GAME_COST_EVIDENCED. Separating a resource from a latch by KIND needs evidence about what the consumer DOES with the value - gates play, feeds a terminal check, or only draws a HUD.
latchVersusResource.consequenceForB3: an action schedule must drive candidate CONSUMERS and not only the candidate own driver, or a field with a consumer and a field with none will look the same. Recorded before B3 rather than discovered during it.
latchVersusResource.readsAreNotEvidence: a difference in read counts or reader sites is a LEAD about consumers, not evidence of a game cost. It is never promoted to GAME_COST_EVIDENCED: HUD code, animation and timers read fields too.

ratioNoise.consequence: rows between about 0.9x and 1.15x are NOT distinguishable from each other or from 1.00. Only the trace row and the whole-zero-page state-sampling row are outside the noise.

eventVolume.note: the single-byte scope sees a handful of events per window and the zero-page scope sees them on every loop iteration. A per-access cost is meaningless without this denominator, and the single-byte rows do NOT establish that unbounded state sampling is affordable.

pacingFloor.note: every mode sits on this floor, so WALL CLOCK RATIOS ARE NOT A COST MEASUREMENT here. --no-max-speed changed nothing when measured directly (6776 ms against 6787 ms over 400 frames), although AgentCli.cpp line 699 sets EmulationFlags::MaximumSpeed by default. Reported as an instrument property, not worked around.

perEventStateSampleCost.conclusion: emu.getState() serialises the whole console, so its cost is per CALL and independent of how little of the result is used. The two-stage scheme is mandatory, not a refinement: cheap aggregated counters for scope, and a bounded number of state samples only for a short causal episode.

overhead.throughputConsequence: at this floor a 2.5 million frame campaign - the size of the S11B corpus - would take roughly 12 hours of wall clock against 47 minutes in jsnes. That bounds what stage B can ask of this instrument and belongs in B5.
